name: Executive order of June 16, 1873 setting apart the Wallowa Valley Reservation for the non-treaty Nez Perce
citation: Executive Order of June 16, 1873 (1 Kappler 894); revoked by Executive Order of June 10, 1875
promises: The President ordered the described tract of the Wallowa Valley in Oregon, from the mouth of the Grande Ronde up the Snake River and back by the Wallowa and Grande Ronde rivers, withheld from entry and settlement as public land and set apart as a reservation for the roaming Nez Perce.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission held that the United States' undertaking to settle Joseph's Band on the 1873 reservation in its homeland created a special relationship imposing an obligation, and concluded as a matter of law that the band had proven a compensable claim for the withdrawal of the Wallowa Reservation, returned to the public domain by the Executive Order of June 10, 1875, to be valued as of that date. Two commissioners dissented in part.

today: In 1941 the Court of Claims (Joseph's Band v. United States, 95 Ct. Cl. 11) rejected the band's claim to aboriginal title to the whole Wallowa-Imnaha area; the Commission held in 1971 that this did not bar the executive order claim. The Commission also found that white settlers on the reservation were not removed while the order stood.

nationVoice.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation (successor to the Joseph Band of Nez Perce)
nationVoice.summary: In 2025 testimony to the Oregon House Committee on Rules, Colville Chairman Jarred-Michael Erickson said the Colville Tribes are the successor government of the Joseph Band, that the band has hunted, fished and gathered in the Wallowa Mountains and valley since time immemorial, and that even after removal its more than 560 descendants on the Colville Reservation still travel to Wallowa County to exercise their treaty rights.

openQuestions: This Royce record is an executive order reservation, not a cession. The revocation alone would not make it broken; the Commission's 1971 liability holding on the Wallowa reservation does.
The Commission's minority said neither Joseph's Band nor other non-treaty bands ever accepted the 1873 reservation or confined themselves to it.

treaties.json lists only the Nez Perce Tribe of Idaho; the Docket 186 claim was brought by the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, where descendants of Joseph's Band live, and the list should probably include them.
The Nez Perce Tribe's and the Colville Tribes' own accounts of the Wallowa reservation were not found on their websites in this pass.
The Wallowa Valley lay within the 1863 treaty cession; the Nez Perce Tribe's recovery for that cession (Docket 175-A) belongs to the 1863 treaty's record.

Audit 2026-11-08: removed the Executive Order of June 10, 1875 as a separate executive-action breach: revoking an executive-order reservation is not by itself a finding. The revocation is now described inside the Commission breach, whose interlocutory order (id 1452) states the compensable claim as a conclusion of law. Status stays broken on that finding.
2026-11-08: counted once with cession-1875-06-10-nez-perc (the Wallowa reservation whose 1875 revocation the Commission found compensable; one taking). The map still shows this row.

plain.promised: In 1873 the President set apart the Wallowa Valley in Oregon, the homeland of Joseph's Band, as a reservation for the non-treaty Nez Perce.
plain.happened: In 1875 the President revoked the order and returned the valley to the public domain. The Indian Claims Commission held in 1971 that this gave Joseph's Band a claim for the value of its interest in that reservation.
plain.today: The claim was settled for $725,000 in 1974, paid to the Colville Tribes on behalf of the Joseph Band.
